title: Shutting DOWN The Stonewall Attack | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: d4 — let's play the knight to f6.
f4 — so this is an attempt at a Stonewall, which has been around a while; White wants to play e3 and c3. There are a couple of things you can do against it: one is d5, controlling the e4-square,
Against the Stonewall, the King's Indian setup works well — you do not need to be a King's Indian player to use it.
let's make the standard King's-Indian moves — the bishop to g7.
and castle — the order doesn't matter; you'll play d6, though castling first was a little more flexible.
The bishop to d3. White may push e4 next and reach a Pirc structure — a setup you can handle comfortably.
So you castle — e4 is nothing to fear.

What's the benefit of the pawn on d6 rather than d5? What idea does d6 prepare? You could play c5, but that's not my favourite — c5 can just be met with c3, much like the London. What you need to prepare is e5 — not immediately, you can't yet — you prepare it with the knight to c6. The point is that when you play e5 you
cause a much bigger explosion in the centre, because you attack both pawns and threaten a fork — so e5 does a lot more than c5 here. Let's get your knight out.

And now you're ready to play e5. You might look at this and say White has three attackers and only two defenders — but if you calculate further, to win the pawn White has to totally ruin their structure,
and you'll win the e5-pawn back very easily. I can show this in more detail after the game, but you can safely play e5 without worrying about losing a pawn.
Your opponent continues to play very fast — the knight to d2. Now you have several options; what's a reasonable follow-up?
The rook to e8 backs up the push e4, and you can open the e-file later.
